items.prose: A sailing club hangs 7 flags in a vertical line as a signal: 4 red, 2 blue and 1 yellow. Flags of one colour look identical, so a signal is the order of the colours from top to bottom.

parts.question: How many different signals are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Label every flag, count the orders, then divide out the relabellings of each colour.

byKey.no-divide: $7! = 5040$ treats every flag as different. Divide by $4!$ for the reds and $2!$ for the blues.
byKey.reds-only: You divided by $4!$ for the reds only. The two blues swap too, so divide by $2!$ as well.
byKey.blues-only: You divided by $2!$ for the blues only. The four reds relabel in $4! = 24$ ways too.

explain.text: With every flag labelled there are $7! = 5040$ orders. The reds relabel in $4! = 24$ ways and the blues in $2! = 2$. So $5040 \div 48 = 105$ signals.

parts.question: In how many signals are the two blue flags next to each other?

feedback.correct: Glue the blues: 6 units, 4 of them red, so $\dfrac{6!}{4!} = 30$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Glue the two blue flags into one unit, then count with the repeats.

byKey.flipped: You doubled for the block facing two ways. The blue flags are identical, so flipping the block changes nothing.
byKey.no-divide: $6! = 720$ treats the 4 reds as different. Divide by $4! = 24$.
byKey.blue-divide: You divided by $2!$ for the blues as well. Once glued they are one unit, so only the reds repeat.

explain.text: The two blues become one unit, leaving 6 units: the block, 4 reds and the yellow. The reds repeat, so there are $6! \div 4! = 720 \div 24 = 30$ orders. The block needs no doubling, because the blues look the same.

parts.question: Using 105 signals and 30 with the blues together, how many signals keep the two blue flags apart?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Every signal has the blues either together or apart.

byKey.carried: That is $105 - 60$, from doubling the block in part 2. With 30 together, $105 - 30 = 75$.
byKey.added: You added the two counts. The together signals are inside the 105, so subtract them.

explain.text: Each signal has the blues together or apart, never both. So the apart signals are $105 - 30 = 75$.

parts.question: The club hangs a signal at random, each of the 105 equally likely. Using 75 from part 3, what is the chance the blue flags are apart? Give a fraction or a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the signals you want over all the signals.

byKey.together: $\tfrac{30}{105} = \tfrac{2}{7}$ is the chance the blues are together. We want them apart.
byKey.carried: That is $\tfrac{45}{105}$, from the doubled block. With 75 apart it is $\tfrac{75}{105}$.
byKey.bottom: You divided by $7! = 5040$, which counts labelled flags. Count the bottom as the top: 105 signals.

explain.text: Every signal is equally likely, so the chance is $\tfrac{75}{105} = \tfrac{5}{7} \approx 0.714$. Check by places: the blues take 2 of 7 places in $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ ways, 6 of them side by side, and $\tfrac{15}{21} = \tfrac{5}{7}$.

items.prose: A leisure centre has 80 members. 45 of them swim, 38 use the gym, and 20 do both.

parts.question: How many members do at least one of the two?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the two groups, then deal with the members counted twice.

byKey.no-overlap: $45 + 38 = 83$ counts the 20 who do both twice. Take them away once.
byKey.twice: You took the 20 away twice. Adding counted them twice, so take them away once: $83 - 20$.

explain.text: Adding $45 + 38$ counts each of the 20 who do both twice. Take them away once: $45 + 38 - 20 = 63$ members do at least one.

parts.question: Using 63 from part 1, how many members do neither?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Neither is the complement of at least one.

byKey.carried: That is $80 - 43$, from taking the 20 away twice. With 63, $80 - 63 = 17$.
byKey.only-one: 43 do exactly one: $25 + 18$. Neither is everyone minus at least one.

explain.text: Every member does at least one of the two, or neither. So neither is $80 - 63 = 17$ members.

parts.question: One member is picked at random, each equally likely. Using 17 from part 2, what is the chance this member does neither? Give a fraction or a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the members you want over all the members.

byKey.at-least: $\tfrac{63}{80}$ is the chance of at least one. Neither is $\tfrac{17}{80}$.
byKey.carried: That is $\tfrac{37}{80}$, from a slip in part 2. With 17 it is $\tfrac{17}{80}$.
byKey.bottom: You divided by 63, the members who do something. The bottom is all 80 members.

explain.text: All 80 members are equally likely, and 17 do neither. So the chance is $\tfrac{17}{80} = 0.2125$.

parts.question: Part 3 gave $\tfrac{17}{80}$ for one member. Now two different members are picked at random for a survey, every pair equally likely. Squaring $\tfrac{17}{80}$ would let one member be picked twice, so count pairs. Using 17 who do neither, what is the chance both do neither? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count pairs on top and pairs on the bottom.

byKey.replaced: $(\tfrac{17}{80})^2$ lets the same member be picked twice. The two are different, so count pairs.
byKey.ordered-top: You put $17 \times 16$ ordered picks over unordered pairs. Count both the same way.
byKey.pairs-over-members: You divided 136 pairs by 80 members. The bottom must count pairs too: $\binom{80}{2} = 3160$.

explain.text: The top is the pairs from the 17: $\binom{17}{2} = 136$. The bottom is all pairs: $\binom{80}{2} = 3160$. So the chance is $\tfrac{136}{3160} \approx 0.043$.

items.prose: A toy shop sells the word BALLOON as seven letter blocks: B, A, two Ls, two Os and N. Blocks with the same letter look identical. A child lays all seven blocks in a row.

parts.question: How many different rows can the child make?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Label the twin blocks, count the orders, then divide out each pair of twins.

byKey.no-divide: $7! = 5040$ treats the twin blocks as different. Divide by $2!$ for the Ls and $2!$ for the Os.
byKey.one-pair: You divided by 2 once. The Ls and the Os each swap, so divide by 2 twice.

explain.text: With every block labelled there are $7! = 5040$ orders. The Ls swap in $2!$ ways and the Os in $2!$ ways. So there are $5040 \div 4 = 1260$ rows.

parts.question: In how many rows are the two Os side by side?

feedback.correct: Glue OO: 6 units with the Ls repeated, $\dfrac{6!}{2!} = 360$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Glue the two Os into one unit, then count with the repeats left.

byKey.flipped: That is 720: either you doubled for the block facing two ways or you forgot the repeated L. The Os look the same, so divide $6!$ by $2!$ for the Ls only.
byKey.both-divided: You divided by 2 for the Os as well. Once glued they are one unit, so only the Ls repeat.

explain.text: The OO block, B, A, L, L and N make 6 units, with the Ls repeated. That gives $6! \div 2! = 720 \div 2 = 360$ rows. Flipping OO changes nothing, so there is no doubling.

parts.question: Using 1260 rows and 360 with the Os together, how many rows have the two Os apart?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apart is everything minus together.

byKey.carried: That is $1260 - 720$, from the doubled block in part 2. With 360, $1260 - 360 = 900$.
byKey.carried-half: That is $1260 - 180$, from dividing by 2 twice in part 2. With 360, $1260 - 360 = 900$.

explain.text: Each row has the Os together or apart. So the rows with the Os apart number $1260 - 360 = 900$.

parts.question: Of the 900 rows with the Os apart, how many also have the two Ls apart?

feedback.correct: Ls together and Os apart is $360 - 120 = 240$, so $900 - 240 = 660$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the rows with the Ls together but the Os apart, and take those away.

byKey.all-ls: You took away all 360 rows with the Ls together. 120 of them have the Os together too, and are not among the 900.
byKey.both-only: You took away only the 120 rows with both pairs together. Those are not among the 900; take away the rows with the Ls together and the Os apart.

explain.text: Glued LL gives $6! \div 2! = 360$ rows, and 120 of them also have OO glued, from $5! = 120$. So 240 rows have the Ls together and the Os apart. Taking them away leaves $900 - 240 = 660$.

parts.question: The child lays the blocks at random, every one of the 1260 rows equally likely. Using 660 from part 4, what is the chance that no two matching blocks touch? Give a fraction or a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the rows you want over all the rows.

byKey.carried: That is $\tfrac{540}{1260}$, from the slip in part 4. With 660 it is $\tfrac{660}{1260}$.
byKey.os-only: $\tfrac{900}{1260}$ only keeps the Os apart. The Ls must be apart too.
byKey.bottom: You divided by $7! = 5040$, which counts labelled blocks. Count the bottom as the top: 1260 rows.

explain.text: Every row is equally likely, so the chance is $\tfrac{660}{1260}$. Cancelling by 60 gives $\tfrac{11}{21} \approx 0.524$.

items.prose: A youth club has 6 girls and 5 boys. Four of them are picked at random to form a quiz team, every group of 4 equally likely.

parts.question: How many different teams of 4 are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite. A team has no order, so count each group of 4 once.

byKey.ordered: $11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8$ counts each team in every order. Divide by $4! = 24$.
byKey.times: You multiplied 11 by 4. Choosing 4 of 11 is $\binom{11}{4}$.

explain.text: In order there are $11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8 = 7920$ picks. Each team appears $4! = 24$ times. So there are $7920 \div 24 = 330$ teams.

parts.question: How many of the teams contain no girls?

feedback.generic: Not quite. A team with no girls takes all 4 members from the boys.

byKey.no-boys: $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ is the teams with no boys. No girls means 4 of the 5 boys.
byKey.ordered: $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2$ puts the boys in order. Divide by $4!$, or note $\binom{5}{4} = \binom{5}{1} = 5$.

explain.text: A team with no girls is 4 of the 5 boys. Choosing 4 to go is choosing 1 to stay, so there are $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ such teams.

parts.question: Using 330 teams in all and 5 with no girls, how many teams have at least one girl?

feedback.correct: At least one girl is all minus none: $330 - 5 = 325$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. At least one is everything minus none.

byKey.no-boys: That is $330 - 15$, which removes the teams with no boys. Remove the 5 with no girls.
byKey.exactly-one: $6 \times \binom{5}{3} = 60$ is exactly one girl. At least one also takes in 2, 3 or 4 girls.

explain.text: Every team has no girls or at least one. So at least one girl is $330 - 5 = 325$ teams.

parts.question: Of the 325 teams with at least one girl, how many also have at least one boy?

feedback.correct: Take off the teams of 4 girls: $325 - \binom{6}{4} = 325 - 15 = 310$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which of the 325 teams have no boy at all?

byKey.no-girls-again: You took off the 5 teams with no girls again. They are already gone. Take off the 15 with no boys.
byKey.both-off: You took off both the 15 and the 5. The 5 with no girls are not among the 325, so take off only 15.

explain.text: Among the 325, the only teams with no boy are the all-girl teams. There are $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ of them, so $325 - 15 = 310$ teams have a girl and a boy.

parts.question: What is the chance the team has at least one girl and at least one boy? Use 310 from part 4. Give a fraction or a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the teams you want over all the teams.

byKey.girl-only: $\tfrac{325}{330}$ is the chance of at least one girl. The team needs a boy too.
byKey.bottom: You divided by 325. Every one of the 330 teams is possible, so the bottom is 330.
byKey.carried: That is $\tfrac{305}{330}$, from the slip in part 4. With 310 it is $\tfrac{310}{330}$.

explain.text: All 330 teams are equally likely and 310 of them mix girls and boys. So the chance is $\tfrac{310}{330} = \tfrac{31}{33} \approx 0.939$.
